steps.prompt: Both sentences say the same thing. Which one makes you lean in? Why?
steps.a: I opened the box and found that there was nothing inside it.
steps.reveal: B uses a dash to create a pause, like a held breath before the surprise. Colons, semicolons and dashes are tools for showing how ideas connect, and for controlling the reader’s pace.

cards.title: The colon: here it comes
cards.body: A colon comes after a complete sentence and points to what follows: a list, an explanation or an example. “I packed three things: a map, a torch and snacks.” “The reason was simple: we were lost.”

cards.title: No colon after a verb
cards.telling: My favourite sports are: soccer, tennis and swimming.
cards.showing: My favourite sports are soccer, tennis and swimming. / I love three sports: soccer, tennis and swimming.
cards.note: Test: cover everything after the colon. Is what’s left a complete sentence? If not, take the colon out.

cards.title: The semicolon: two linked sentences
cards.text:
The storm hit; the lights went out.
We were exhausted; however, we kept climbing.
Not: The storm hit; and the lights went out. (a semicolon or “and”, not both)
cards.note: Both sides of a semicolon must be complete sentences that are closely linked.

cards.title: The dash: a sudden break
cards.body: A dash (—) adds a dramatic pause or an extra detail: “We had one job — win the game.” A pair of dashes can work like a pair of commas: “My cousin — the one who plays drums — is visiting.” In essays, use one or two at most.

prompts: Which mark (colon, semicolon or dash) feels most useful for your essays? Why?
How is a semicolon different from a comma?
